title: Scope
text: edgeslm fine-tunes small language models (SLMs) for narrow tasks and runs them on edge hardware. This page describes the approach through its first task: short WhatsApp messages that tell coffee farmers which plants are short of water and which sensors need fixing. It is a working document, and its sections change as we refine the approach.

title: Scope
text:
Problem and framing
A large hosted model can already do an expert’s analysis. In the batch 2 diagnosis of speaking-plants, Claude found the water-stressed plant from the sensor logs, much as a plant physiologist would. Using such a model for every message in the field has costs:

every call costs money and energy,
farm data leaves the farm,
the service depends on a provider, and on the network at the moment of the call,
a narrow, repeated task uses only a small part of the model’s expertise.

edgeslm takes the other route: a small model, fine-tuned for one narrow task, that runs on a board on the farm. The model is like a chip that holds one slice of domain expertise. The pipeline that builds it is domain-neutral: a task is defined by data, namely its input format, its output format and its examples.

The first task
The first task comes from speaking-plants, which detects water stress in coffee plants with thermal cameras, soil moisture sensors and an air sensor. Sensors are costly to run, so only some plants carry a sensor node: a farm can have dozens of nodes, each standing for the plants around it. The task has two parts:

Triage, in code. Feature engineering and a classical ML model decide, for one farm and one day, which nodes to watch or fix, how severe each case is, and what the data shows about its cause, such as whether water still reaches the soil. This part belongs to the domain project, not to edgeslm.
The message, by the SLM. The model turns the triage into a short WhatsApp message to the farmer.

Deciding what is critical is the code’s job. Saying it clearly, with an action, is the model’s job.
The message follows these rules:

It covers only the nodes to watch or fix. When nothing is critical, nothing is sent.
It says what to do, such as watering or maintenance. It gives no measurements or counts: a value such as a leaf-to-air temperature difference means little to a farmer as an absolute number, and the engineered features and the ML model already capture the signal. A count of flagged nodes would mislead too, because only some plants are monitored and a problem on a shared line usually reaches the plants between them.
It covers two kinds of problem: water stress, and equipment faults such as a failed sensor or a silent node.
Each item is one paragraph: its severity marker, its location exactly as in the triage, a colon, then what is wrong and what to do. The markers are 👀 early, ⚠️ moderate and 🚨 severe. Later mentions use words such as “the line” or “its dripper”, not the location again.
Its paragraphs follow the triage’s order, most severe first, and say when each problem started with the triage’s phrase, such as since today, since Tuesday or for a week or more. It never gives a date.
It is at most 600 characters long, so that it fits on a phone screen.
It is sent in the evening or early in the morning, before irrigation. Water stress shows most clearly in the afternoon.

Here is a sketch of one triage output and its message, for an invented farm with 40 sensor nodes. The triage contract, below, defines its fields and rules:
{
  "farm": "fazenda-exemplo", "date": "2026-10-08", "nodes": 40,
  "items": [
    {"problem": "water stress", "location": "Block B, drip line B2", "pattern": "cluster",
     "nodes_flagged": 6, "nodes_in_group": 8, "severity": "moderate", "since": "since Tuesday",
     "soil_water": "none since Tuesday"},
    {"problem": "equipment fault", "location": "Block A, row 1", "pattern": "one node",
     "severity": "moderate", "since": "since Monday", "fault": "missing data"},
    {"problem": "water stress", "location": "Block C, row 3", "pattern": "one node",
     "severity": "early", "since": "since today", "soil_water": "arriving"}
  ]
}

⚠️ Block B, drip line B2: most monitored plants have been short of water since Tuesday, and no water has reached their soil since then. Check the line today, from its start to the last plant.
⚠️ Block A, row 1: the sensors at this plant have sent no data since Monday, so it is not monitored. Check the node’s power and connection.
👀 Block C, row 3: a monitored plant has shown first signs of water stress since today, although its soil still gets water. Check the plant for heat damage or root problems.



Language
The farmers in the first task read Brazilian Portuguese. Small models are usually weaker in Portuguese than in English, so the baseline measures candidate models in Portuguese before any fine-tuning. Fine-tuning should help: it picks up style and vocabulary from little data, and regional farm vocabulary is that kind of target. If small models still fall short, a fixed template can carry the locations, markers and actions, and the model writes only the rest. The proof of concept uses English.


Hardware
The model runs with llama.cpp on the gateway, the board that collects the nodes’ data over LoRa radio. Two boards are candidates. Rovai compared both with the same models and the same llama.cpp build:

The UNO Q comes in a 2 GB and a 4 GB version. The 4 GB version (ABX00173) has 4 GB of LPDDR4 memory and 32 GB of eMMC storage, and costs €82.90 with VAT on the Arduino store in November 2026. The memory estimates in this section are for the 4 GB version.
Messages are generated once a day per farm, so speed is not the main limit. On the UNO Q, Qwen3.5 2B generated 2.53 tokens per second, so a message of about 100 tokens takes under a minute. Memory sets the limit instead: by our estimate, about 4B parameters on the Pi 5 and about 2B on the UNO Q. The choice of board follows from the evaluation: the smallest model that meets the quality threshold decides the cheapest board that can run it. The fine-tuned Qwen3.5 0.8B passes every check in 264 of the 270 test messages and fits in the UNO Q’s memory, so the UNO Q is the target board.
The fine-tuned model needs only the triage record and a one-line instruction, with no rules or examples. On the UNO Q, the A53 cores must process the whole prompt before they write the message. By our estimate, the untuned models’ prompt of about 1,300 tokens would take longer to process than the message takes to write. The run on the board will measure this.
Sending a WhatsApp message needs a network connection, so a hosted model would often be reachable too. The case for a local model rests on the other reasons: data stays on the farm, there is no cost per message, energy use is low, nothing depends on a provider, and generation does not wait for the network, because the gateway can queue the message until the connection is back.

title: Scope
text:
Pipeline
Building a model for a task follows these stages:

Synthetic triage inputs, sampled across the task’s dimensions, as the next section describes.
Teacher messages: a large model, Claude, writes the message for each input.
Baseline: candidate base models write messages for the test inputs before any fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning: LoRA adapters trained on pairs of inputs and messages. On Apple Silicon this uses MLX; on CUDA GPUs, tools such as unsloth do the same job. The fine-tuned model is prompted with the triage record and a one-line instruction: it learns the rules and the format from the examples.
Evaluation of the baseline and fine-tuned models on the same held-out test set.
Export: the adapter is fused into the base model and converted to GGUF, the single-file format that llama.cpp loads.
Deployment on the target board with llama.cpp, and a final evaluation there.

Domain experts improve the data at stages 1, 2 and 5.
Over time, the two kinds of model take different roles. A large model is the teacher during development, and handles new kinds of cases when a connection is available. The small model handles the repeated task in the field.

Choice of teacher
Claude Haiku writes the teacher messages. Sonnet’s judgement of actions and urgency looked somewhat better on a first batch of ten inputs, at about three times the cost, so the first training set has a message from each model for each of its 200 inputs. The two models wrote the same message, word for word, for 73 of the 200 inputs, and their messages are 92% similar on average: the rules and examples leave little room for a model’s own judgement. A comparison of the two teachers would measure almost nothing, so the cheaper one, Haiku, is the teacher from now on, and the student trains on its messages.
Each message records the model that wrote it, the temperature, the version of the prompt and the date, so that messages written with different prompts are never compared.

title: Scope
text:
Synthetic data generation
Synthetic inputs follow the method of synthetic questions for MARIS: find the dimensions along which cases vary, give each a few levels, and sample combinations of levels, called tuples. Each tuple stands for a distinct case the model must handle. A few dimensions keep every tuple covered. Ten dimensions with a few levels each would give tens of thousands of tuples, most of them never sampled.
The first task has three dimensions with three levels each, so 27 tuples:







Dimension
Levels




Problem
water stress, equipment fault, both


Spatial pattern
one node, a cluster sharing a line or block, widespread


Severity
early, moderate, severe



The levels mean different things for the two kinds of problem:

Spatial pattern. For water stress, one node points to a single plant or dripper, a cluster to a shared irrigation line, and widespread stress to the weather or the irrigation schedule. soil_water tells these apart: when water still arrives, the weather is the likelier cause. For equipment faults, one node points to that node, a cluster to what its nodes share, such as their power supply, and widespread faults to the gateway.
Severity. For water stress, it is the plant’s state: first signs (early), stress for several days (moderate), or a risk of damage (severe). For equipment faults, it is how long and how badly data is lost, whatever the spatial pattern: data missing for hours, implausible values or a changed camera view (early), no data for 1 to 3 days (moderate), or no data for more than 3 days (severe).

A node that sends no readings cannot be flagged for water stress, as the triage contract below requires, because there is no data to detect stress from. So when a both record has a widespread pattern and a moderate or severe severity, the widespread item is the water stress, and the fault is a single node or a cluster. With this rule all 27 tuples are valid, and a widespread, severe fault is a farm left unmonitored for days.
Other variation changes the details of a message but not its kind, so it is drawn at random within each tuple rather than made a dimension: farm size, how locations are named (blocks and rows, numbered plots, greenhouse benches), how long the problem has lasted, and the number of items.
The test set has 10 inputs per tuple, 270 in total, and no test input is ever used for training. Training sets are sampled across all tuples, so scores can be broken down by tuple to show which cases a model gets wrong.

title: Scope
text:
Triage contract
The proof of concept replaces the domain project’s triage with generated records, from 01_coffee. The generator is a mock, but every rule it follows to keep records consistent is also a requirement on the real triage. This section lists the fields and rules, so that the domain project and edgeslm agree on what the triage delivers. The generator is the executable form of this contract: its tests check every rule on every record of the test set.

Fields
One record covers one farm and one day:



Field
Meaning




farm, date
The farm, and the day of the triage.


nodes
The number of sensor nodes on the farm.


items
One entry per problem to watch or fix, most severe first.



Each item has these fields:



Field
Meaning




problem
water stress or equipment fault.


location
A place the farmer knows: one node, a group of nodes on a shared irrigation line, or the whole farm.


pattern
one node, cluster or widespread.


severity
early, moderate or severe, as defined under Synthetic data generation.


since
When the problem started, as a phrase the message can use as it is: since today, since yesterday, since a weekday within the past week, or for a week or more.


soil_water
For water stress only: whether water still reaches the soil, from irrigation or rain. arriving means it does, so more water may not help. Otherwise a phrase such as none since Tuesday means the soil is drying, so water is not reaching the plants.


fault
For equipment faults only: what the data shows. missing data means a node sends nothing, implausible values means a sensor reports values no plant or weather could produce, such as a soil moisture drop too fast for uptake, and camera view changed means the thermal camera no longer sees the same leaves.


sensor
For implausible values only: soil moisture, thermal camera, air temperature or humidity.


nodes_flagged, nodes_in_group
For clusters and widespread items only: how many nodes of the group are flagged, out of how many.


amount
For clusters and widespread items only: the word for the share of flagged nodes, which the message uses as it is: all, almost all (80% or more), most (more than half) or some (half or fewer).





Rules

Readable locations. Locations are names the farmer uses, such as a block and drip line, a row, a plot or a bench. They are never node IDs.
Groups follow irrigation. A cluster is a group of nodes on one irrigation line or valve, so that its action, such as checking the line, reaches all the plants it covers.
One location, one item. No two items point at the same node or group.
Most severe first. Items are sorted by severity, most severe first, so that the message can keep their order.
Aggregation. When one kind of problem flags more than 70% of the farm’s nodes, the triage reports one widespread item with one cause, not several local ones. The single nodes and clusters of one kind stay below that threshold.
No stress without data. A node that sends no readings is reported as a fault, and is never flagged for water stress.
Observed causes. A water stress item says through soil_water whether water reaches the soil, which the soil sensors show directly as a rise after irrigation or rain. The message gives the action at the level the data supports, such as checking the line, and never names a part that no sensor watches, such as a valve. An equipment fault item says through fault what the data shows, and sensor names the sensor when values are implausible. Its action says where to look, by pattern: one node, that node; several nodes, what they share, such as the gateway or the power supply.
No raw values. Weather, readings and engineered features stay inside the ML model. They reach the triage only through severity, since, soil_water, fault and sensor. Raw values in the triage would invite the SLM to reason about them, which is the code’s job.

Some rules need more than sensor data. Readable locations need a map from each node to its place on the farm. Groups need the irrigation layout of each farm. soil_water needs no labels, because the soil sensors show whether water arrives: the batch 2 diagnosis found that watering had stopped from the missing morning rise in soil moisture. Faults need no labels either: fault records what the data shows, and never a cause no sensor watches, such as an empty battery or a lost radio link. The node map and the irrigation layout are the main open questions for the design of the ML side.

title: Scope
text:
Domain expert annotators
Synthetic data and a teacher model are a start. Domain knowledge enters through experts, who:

audit the dimensions and tuples, and say which cases are missing or unrealistic,
review and edit synthetic messages: an edited message becomes better training data, and the difference from the draft shows where the teacher’s judgement is weak,
do error analysis on model outputs, by writing a free-text note on what is wrong (open coding) and then grouping the notes into failure modes (axial coding),
label outputs as pass or fail for each failure mode, to align the judges described under Evaluation,
write messages for real cases, in the same format.

Experts start from drafts rather than blank pages, which is faster and gives more consistent messages. For the first task, they must read and write Brazilian Portuguese.
The dataset of expert-reviewed examples is the lasting artifact, not the model. Each model is rebuilt from a version of the dataset, so it is always possible to say whose expertise, from which version of the data, went into which model.
A minimal annotation app, built with FastHTML and storing its data in SQLite, supports this work. It shows one triage input next to its message. The expert can edit the message, mark it as pass or fail, and write a note.

title: Scope
text:
Evaluation
Evaluation decides whether a model is good enough, and so which board it needs. Three rules hold throughout:

every model, including the untuned base model, is scored on the same held-out test set,
once expert-reviewed examples exist, the test set is weighted towards them, because synthetic data can train a model but should not be its final judge,
final scores are measured on the target board.


Checks computed by code
Some failure modes can be checked by comparing a message with its triage input, without any labels:

Format: every paragraph starts with a marker and a location, followed by a colon.
Coverage: every item in the input has its paragraph.
No invented items: every paragraph names a location from the input, and no location has two paragraphs.
Severity: each paragraph has the marker of its item’s severity, 👀, ⚠️ or 🚨.
No numbers: the message contains no digits outside its locations, so no readings, counts or dates. Numbers that are part of a location, such as row 3, are allowed.
Length: the message is at most 600 characters long.
Amount: each cluster or widespread item uses its record’s amount word.



Judges for the other failure modes
Other failure modes need judgement, such as whether the action fits what the triage reports. They follow the method of LLM as a judge:

Error analysis by experts finds the failure modes.
Each failure mode gets its own judge, a large model that labels a message as pass or fail for that one failure mode.
Expert labels are split into a training set (10 to 20%, for few-shot examples in the judge’s prompt), a development set (40 to 45%, to refine the prompt) and a test set (40 to 45%). No example moves between sets.
On the test set, the judge’s true positive rate (TPR, the share of good messages it passes) and true negative rate (TNR, the share of bad messages it fails) are measured against the expert labels.
The judge’s observed pass rate on new messages is corrected with the Rogan-Gladen formula, which needs TPR + TNR > 1:

\[\theta = \frac{\text{observed rate} + \text{TNR} - 1}{\text{TPR} + \text{TNR} - 1}\]

A bootstrap over the test set gives a 95% confidence interval for the corrected rate.

title: Scope
text:
Proof of concept
The proof of concept is for a meeting, and has four aims:

Explain the setup and why: the use case, and the problem it addresses.
Show that an SLM can be fine-tuned for the task, and how much data it needs.
Explain the role of domain experts: auditing and improving synthetic data, annotating new data, and error analysis for the judges.
Show why AI at the edge suits this task: hosted LLM inference costs money and energy, farm data is sensitive, and the task needs only a small part of a large model’s expertise.

It uses synthetic data only, in English. The expert phase is explained rather than run, and the annotation app shows how it would work. The steps:

Schema and sampler: the triage JSON schema, the 27 tuples, and random variation within each.
Teacher messages: Claude Haiku writes the message for each sampled input, as described under Choice of teacher, and a sample is checked by hand.
Baseline: candidate base models of about 2B parameters or smaller, so that they run on the UNO Q, are scored on the 270 test inputs.
Metric: the checks computed by code. A breakdown by tuple is not done yet.
Fine-tuning: LoRA with MLX on Apple Silicon, trained on 50, 100 and 199 examples, where 199 is every Haiku message in the training set that passes the checks. The scores against the number of examples form a learning curve, which answers how much data the task needs. With 100 examples, both models pass every check in 255 or more of the 270 test messages, so the proof of concept does not train on larger sets.
Export and edge demo: the best model is converted to GGUF, run with llama.cpp, and handed to a colleague with an Arduino UNO Q, with example inputs, the prompt and the command, to measure speed and memory on the board.
Annotation app: the minimal FastHTML app, shown on a few synthetic examples.
Presentation, built from the results of steps 3 to 7.

title: Scope
text:
After the proof of concept
The proof of concept makes one pass through the pipeline on synthetic data. The project then repeats the pipeline in rounds, on two tracks that run side by side: the triage track builds the input, and the message track builds the model that writes the message. The triage contract is the only interface between them.

The triage track
The domain project keeps collecting sensor data on the farms and develops the triage: the features, the ML model, and the node map and irrigation layout listed as open questions under Triage contract. Until the real triage is ready, the generator in 01_coffee stands in for it. When it is ready, its records join the generated ones, first as test inputs and then as training inputs. A change to the contract, such as a new field or a new kind of fault, starts a new round on the message track.


The message track
Each round on the message track has these steps:

Inputs: synthetic triage records, and real ones as the triage produces them. Experts audit the dimensions and tuples and name the missing cases.
Messages: the teacher drafts a message for each input. Experts review and edit a sample in the annotation app, and their edited messages replace the drafts in the training set.
Fine-tuning: the small model is trained on the current version of the dataset.
Evaluation: the code checks run on every message. Experts annotate a sample of the small model’s messages, first with free-text notes and then with a pass or fail for each failure mode, as described under Domain expert annotators. Once there are enough expert labels, an LLM judge for each failure mode, aligned on those labels, scores the failure modes that code cannot check.
Deployment: the model is exported to GGUF, scored again on the board, and installed on the gateways.
Field review: experts review a sample of the messages written on real farms, and those cases enter the next round.

Each round ends with a new version of the dataset and the model built from it. Failure modes found in error analysis become new code checks or judges, and missing cases become new tuples.

title: Scope
text:
Terms

SLM: small language model, here with up to about 4 billion parameters.
LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation, a fine-tuning method that trains small adapter matrices next to the frozen weights of a model. Not to be confused with LoRa, the long-range radio that links the nodes to the gateway. In code, we avoid a bare lora name.
GGUF: the single-file model format of llama.cpp, holding the weights, usually quantized, with the tokenizer and metadata.
Node: a sensor station on one plant, which stands for the plants around it. Only some plants carry one.
Triage: the output of the domain code, listing the nodes to watch or fix for one farm and one day.
Tuple: one combination of levels, one from each dimension.
Teacher: the large model that writes reference messages.
Failure mode: one specific way a message can be wrong, found by error analysis.

title: Export
text: The Arduino UNO Q runs models with llama.cpp, which loads GGUF files. This notebook turns the fine-tuned Qwen3.5 0.8B from Fine-tuning, trained on 199 examples, into GGUF files at 8 and 4 bits, and scores each one on the test set through llama.cpp. The scores must match the MLX model’s before a file goes to the board.

title: Export
text:
Merging the adapter
mlx-lm’s own GGUF export supports only Llama, Mistral and Mixtral models, so the GGUF file comes from llama.cpp’s converter, convert_hf_to_gguf.py. The converter reads checkpoints in the Hugging Face layout. The mlx-community checkpoint we trained on is not in that layout: its tensor names start with language_model.model. instead of model.language_model., its vision encoder is removed, and its convolution weights are transposed.
The adapter changes only linear projections, and the base weights of those 124 projections are identical in the two checkpoints. fuse_lora therefore merges the adapter into the original Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B checkpoint. It renames each adapted layer and adds scale · Bᵀ·Aᵀ to its weight, the formula mlx-lm uses when it fuses. The other files of the checkpoint are copied unchanged:


source

fuse_lora
def fuse_lora(
    base:str, # Directory of the original Hugging Face checkpoint
    adapters:str, # Directory of the mlx-lm adapters
    out:str, # Directory for the merged checkpoint
)->pathlib._local.Path:
Merge mlx-lm LoRA adapters into a Hugging Face checkpoint


We checked the merge by loading the merged checkpoint with mlx-lm: it wrote the same messages as the adapter for the first three test records.
This cell merged the adapter and converted the result. It needs the export extra (pip install -e '.[export]'), llama.cpp’s command-line tools (brew install llama.cpp, version 0.8.0 here) and a checkout of llama.cpp at the same commit for convert_hf_to_gguf.py, and does not run in tests:

import subprocess, sys
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download
LLAMA_CPP = Path('~/pro/dev/llama.cpp').expanduser()
run = Path('../models/qwen3.5-0.8b-n199')
hf = fuse_lora(snapshot_download('Qwen/Qwen3.5-0.8B'), run/'adapters', run/'hf')
gguf = run/'gguf'; gguf.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
bf16 = gguf/'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-bf16.gguf'
subprocess.run([sys.executable, LLAMA_CPP/'convert_hf_to_gguf.py', hf, '--outtype', 'bf16', '--outfile', bf16], env={'PYTHONPATH': str(LLAMA_CPP/'gguf-py')}, check=True)
for q in ('Q8_0', 'Q4_K_M'): subprocess.run(['llama-quantize', bf16, gguf/f'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-{q}.gguf', q], check=True)

title: Export
text:
Scoring with llama.cpp
score_gguf sends each test record to a running llama-server and checks the message. It builds the prompt with student_input, the same chat-formatted string the MLX runs used, and decodes greedily. Any change in score therefore comes from llama.cpp and the quantization. Each row also keeps llama.cpp’s token counts and timings:


source

score_gguf
async def score_gguf(
    url:str, # Address of a running `llama-server`
    rows:list, # Test rows with `id`, `tuple` and `record`
    tok, # The model's tokenizer, to build the chat-formatted prompt
    name:str, # Name of the GGUF file, saved in each row
    n_par:int=4, # Requests in flight at once
    max_tokens:int=400, # Longest message to generate
)->list: # One row per input, with the message, its checks and llama.cpp's timings
Have a llama.cpp server write and check a message for each row


This cell scored each file, with llama-server -m <file> --port 8091 -c 4096 -np 4 running in a terminal. It does not run in tests:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from edgeslm.dataset import read_jsonl, write_jsonl
test = read_jsonl('../data/test-v1.jsonl')
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained('../models/qwen3.5-0.8b-n199/hf')
q = 'Q4_K_M'  # restart the server with each file, then set q to match
write_jsonl(f'../data/gguf-v1-qwen3.5-0.8b-n199-{q}.jsonl', await score_gguf('http://localhost:8091', test, tok, f'qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-{q}.gguf'))

title: Export
text:
Running on the UNO Q
The colleague with the board needs llama.cpp built on it, the 4-bit file qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf, and the folder data/uno-q from this repo. The folder holds three test prompts, prompt-N.txt, already in the model’s chat format, and the 4-bit file’s message for each, expected-N.txt. This cell wrote them, and does not run in tests:

for i in range(3):
    Path(f'../data/uno-q/prompt-{i}.txt').write_text(student_input(tok, test[i]['record'], SHORT_PROMPT))
    Path(f'../data/uno-q/expected-{i}.txt').write_text(q4[i]['message'])

The steps below run on the board. First, build llama.cpp at the version used here (0.8.0) on the board’s Debian:
sudo apt install git cmake build-essential time
git clone https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp && cd llama.cpp
git checkout 8642541b2
cmake -B build && cmake --build build --config Release -j 4
The tools are in build/bin. Copy the GGUF file and the uno-q folder next to them, then run each step from build/bin.
Check the download. The checksum must match before anything else:
sha256sum qwen3.5-0.8b-edgeslm-Q4_K_M.gguf
# 4f283f2f87413fe1c3cdb83f226c8cdf3c31eae7dc456c268a702ba0a7c63769
A different value means the download is incomplete or the file has changed. Download it again.

Measure speed. Test prompts average 168 tokens and messages 71, so benchmark those sizes on the four cores:

Send back the three outputs, the llama-bench table and the peak memory.

On the computer, run the scoring cell above with the board’s address, http://<board-ip>:8091, and n_par=1, so that each timing measures one message on its own. Each row then holds the board’s timings for that message. We have not run this yet.

title: Fine-tuning
text: Fine-tuning trains LoRA adapters with mlx-lm on Haiku’s messages. Each model is trained on 50, 100 and 199 examples, and scored on the frozen test set with the code checks, like the baseline; the scores against the number of examples form the learning curve of the scope.

title: Fine-tuning
text:
Training data
teacher_rows keeps Haiku’s messages that passed every check, in one fixed random order. A training set of n examples is the first n rows, so each smaller set is part of the larger ones and the curve reflects size, not a different draw:


source

teacher_rows

    rows:list, # Labelled rows from `label_all`
    seed:int=0, # Seed of the fixed order
)->list:
The rows by TEACHER that pass every check, in a fixed random order

The fine-tuned models get a one-line instruction, SHORT_PROMPT, instead of the baseline’s student prompt, for two reasons. Training on Qwen3.5 with the student prompt ran out of memory on a 32 GB M5, even one example at a time: an example with the full prompt is 1,304 tokens, and the memory that training needs grows steeply with length. With the short prompt an example is about 165 tokens and trains easily. On the board, a short prompt also saves reading 1,300 tokens before every message. The model learns the rules from the examples instead of reading them, which is what fine-tuning is for.
mlx-lm reads chat rows: the instruction as the system message, the record as the user message, and the teacher’s message as the reply. Qwen3.5’s chat template writes the reply after the same empty thinking block that student_input ends with, so training text starts exactly with the text the model sees at inference:

title: Fine-tuning
text:
Training
lora_cmd builds the command that runs mlx-lm’s trainer as a separate process. Every run uses the same settings: mlx-lm’s default rank, layers and maximum length, a learning rate of 1e-4, and 4 epochs. Training Qwen3.5 in mlx-lm takes far more memory than a model of this size should: batches of 4 short examples, about 1,200 tokens, ran out of memory on a 32 GB M5. Each step therefore takes one example, with gradient checkpointing, and the weights update every 4 steps, which matches batches of 4 for the optimiser. Only the reply counts in the loss, and validation runs once per epoch:


source

lora_cmd
def lora_cmd(
    model_id:str, # Hugging Face id of the MLX model
    data:str, # Directory written by `write_mlx_data`
    adapters:str, # Directory for the trained adapters
    n:int, # Number of training examples
    accum:int=4, # Examples per weight update, one at a time
    epochs:int=4, # Passes over the training set
    lr:float=0.0001, # Learning rate
)->list: # The command, as arguments for `subprocess.run`
The mlx-lm command that trains LoRA adapters for model_id on data


This cell trained the six adapters and scored each one on the test set, and does not run in tests. On an Apple M5 with 32 GB, training took about 2 hours and scoring about 80 minutes. for name, mid in MODELS.items():
    for n in (50, 100, 199):
        run = f'{name}-n{n}'
        write_mlx_data(f'../models/{run}/data', train[:n], valid)
        res = subprocess.run(lora_cmd(mid, f'../models/{run}/data', f'../models/{run}/adapters', n), capture_output=True, text=True, check=True)
        Path(f'../models/{run}/train.log').write_text(re.sub(r'\x1b\[[0-9;?]*[A-Za-z]', '', res.stdout))
        write_jsonl(f'../data/finetune-v1-{run}.jsonl', run_model(mid, test, adapter_path=f'../models/{run}/adapters', sp=SHORT_PROMPT))

title: Synthetic data
text: A task’s synthetic inputs should cover every kind of case the model must handle, not drift towards the common ones. Following synthetic questions for MARIS, we list the dimensions along which cases vary, give each a few levels, and sample tuples: combinations of one level from each dimension. Each tuple stands for one distinct kind of case. This module holds the part every task shares; each task supplies its own dimensions and a generator that turns a tuple into one input.

title: Synthetic data

Tuples
Dimensions are a dict from dimension name to its levels. The MARIS dimensions make a small example:

             complexity=['direct factual', 'analytical', 'conceptual'])

tuples

    dims:dict, # Dimension name -> its levels

title: Synthetic data
text:
Sampling
sample calls the task’s generator gen(tuple, rng) n times. It cycles through the tuples in a shuffled order, so each tuple gets n // len(tuples) inputs or one more: 270 inputs over 27 tuples gives exactly 10 each, and 50 inputs gives 1 or 2 each. All randomness comes from one random.Random(seed) passed to the generator, so a seed reproduces the whole set. Different seeds give the independent draws needed for separate training and test sets.

sample
def sample(
    dims:dict, # Dimension name -> its levels
    gen, # `gen(tuple, rng)` returns one input for `tuple`
    n:int, # Number of inputs
    seed:int=0, # Seed of the random generator passed to `gen`
)->list[dict]: # Dicts with the `tuple` and the generated `input`
n inputs from gen, spread evenly over the tuples of dims

title: edgeslm
text:
edgeslm fine-tunes small language models (SLMs) for narrow, domain-specific tasks, and runs them on edge hardware such as a Raspberry Pi 5 or an Arduino UNO Q. A large hosted model can do the same tasks, but every call costs money and energy, data leaves the site, and the service depends on a provider and a network. A narrow task that repeats every day uses only a small part of a large model’s expertise, so a small model trained for it can do the job locally.
The pipeline is domain-neutral: a task is defined by data, namely its input format, its output format and its examples. It goes from synthetic inputs and outputs written by a large teacher model, through LoRA fine-tuning and evaluation, to a GGUF model that llama.cpp runs on the board. The approach is described, and refined as the project goes, in Scope.

title: edgeslm
text:
The first task
The first task comes from speaking-plants, which detects water stress in coffee plants with sensor nodes. Each day, code in the domain project produces a triage for each farm: which nodes to watch or fix, how severe each problem is, and what the data shows about its cause, such as whether water still reaches the soil. The SLM turns the triage into a short WhatsApp message for the farmer, with an action for each problem.
The real triage does not exist yet, so coffee generates synthetic records that follow the triage contract in the scope, using the tuple sampler in synth. Here is one record:

triage(dict(problem='water stress', pattern='cluster', severity='moderate'), random.Random(0))

{'farm': 'Fazenda São João',
 'date': '2026-05-17',
 'nodes': 45,
 'items': [{'problem': 'water stress',
   'location': 'Block B, drip line B1',
   'pattern': 'cluster',
   'severity': 'moderate',
   'since': 'since Friday',
   'soil_water': 'arriving',
   'nodes_flagged': 6,
   'nodes_in_group': 7,
   'amount': 'almost all'}]}


A message for this record could read:

⚠️ Block B, drip line B1: almost all monitored plants have shown water stress since Friday, although their soil still gets water. Check the plants on this line for heat damage or root problems.

title: edgeslm
text:
Status
The project is building a proof of concept for the first task. The scope, the synthetic triage records, the code checks, the teacher prompt and the training data are done. Claude Haiku wrote the training messages.
The baseline and fine-tuning experiments compare Qwen3.5 0.8B and 2B on 270 test records. Untuned, with rules and two examples in the prompt, they write messages that pass every check for 123 and 70 records. Fine-tuned on 100 examples, with a one-line prompt, both pass for 255 or more. The 0.8B fine-tuned on 199 examples passes for 264.
The fine-tuned 0.8B is exported to GGUF for llama.cpp. At 4 bits the file is 542 MB and still passes for 264 of the 270 records. The next step is to run it on an Arduino UNO Q and measure speed, memory and quality on the board. Running on the UNO Q gives the steps for the colleague with the board.

title: edgeslm
text:
Install
Install the latest version from GitHub:
pip install git+https://github.com/franckalbinet/edgeslm.git

title: Message checks
text: The scope lists failure modes that code can check by comparing a message with its triage record, with no labels needed. This module implements them for the first task. The same checks screen the teacher’s messages before they become training data, and score the base and fine-tuned models, broken down by tuple.

A message that keeps every rule has one paragraph per item. Each paragraph starts with the item’s marker and its location exactly as in the record, then a colon, then what is wrong and what to do:

msg = """🚨 Plot 1: some monitored plants in this plot have been short of water since Saturday, and no water has reached their soil since Friday. Check this plot's irrigation line today, from its start to the last plant.

⚠️ Plot 2: most sensors in this plot have sent no data since Sunday, so the plants they cover are not monitored. Check the power supply these sensors share.

👀 Plot 3, row 1: the camera at this plant has not seen its leaves since today. Check that it points at the plant and that nothing blocks its view."""

title: Message checks
text:
Parsing
parse splits a message into paragraphs, and reads the marker, location and text of each. Models sometimes drop the invisible variation selector that follows ⚠ in ⚠️, so parse accepts the marker with or without it.


source

parse
def parse(
    msg:str, # A message, with one paragraph per item
)->list: # (marker, location, text) for each paragraph, or `None` for one not in that format
Split msg into its items




Exported source

test_eq([(m, l) for m, l, _ in ps], [('🚨', 'Plot 1'), ('⚠️', 'Plot 2'), ('👀', 'Plot 3, row 1')])

 'Plot 1',
 "some monitored plants in this plot have been short of water since Saturday, and no water has reached their soil since Friday. Check this plot's irrigation line today, from its start to the last plant.")


A paragraph without a marker and a location gives None:

title: Message checks
text:
Checks
check runs the checks of the scope, and returns whether each passed:

format: every paragraph has a marker and a location.
coverage: every item of the record has its paragraph.
no_invented: every paragraph names a location from the record, and no location has two paragraphs.
severity: each paragraph has the marker of its item’s severity.
no_numbers: no digits outside the record’s locations, so no readings, counts or dates.
length: at most MAX_LEN characters.
amount: each cluster or widespread item uses its record’s amount word.

Locations are compared without case, so that “Whole farm” at the start of a paragraph matches whole farm.

title: Teacher prompt
text:
The teacher is a large model, Claude, that writes the message for each synthetic triage record. Its messages are the training targets for the SLM, so this prompt defines what a good message is. It follows the structure of write_prose: rules, good examples, one bad message with its mistakes marked, a numbered list of failure modes, and plain words to use. The SLM never sees this prompt. Fine-tuning builds the behaviour into it, so the prompt’s length only costs the teacher, and prompt caching covers most of that.
The failure modes are shared. The code checks in checks cover some of them, and the judges and the annotation app will use the same list for the rest, until expert error analysis replaces it.

title: Teacher prompt
text:
Rules
The rules restate the message rules of the scope for the teacher. The triage contract keeps them simple: items arrive most severe first, and since is a phrase to copy.
The context and rules, as the teacher reads them:

Markdown(f'{CONTEXT}\n\n{RULES}')

You write short WhatsApp messages to coffee farmers. Each message turns one triage record into actions. The record comes from monitoring code, which has already decided which problems matter, how severe they are, and what the data shows about their cause. Only some plants carry a sensor, and each sensor stands for the plants around it.

Write one paragraph per item, in the record’s order.
Start each paragraph with the item’s marker (👀 early, ⚠️ moderate, 🚨 severe), then its location exactly as written in the record, then a colon.
After the colon, say in plain words what is wrong and when it started, then what to do. Say only what the record reports, and never name a cause or a part it does not report, such as a valve, a battery or a radio link. Never write likely, may, might or probably.
Say when the problem started with the record’s since phrase, as it is. When soil_water has the same phrase, say it once, such as “have had no water and shown water stress for a week or more”.
After the location, refer to it with words such as “this line”, “this plot” or “this plant”. Never repeat the location or part of it.
Write no digits outside the locations: no readings, counts or dates. Speak of monitored plants. For a single node, say “a monitored plant” or “this plant”.
Every cluster or widespread item has an amount word: all, almost all, most or some. Use it as it is, even when it is all, as in “all monitored plants on this line”.
For water stress, soil_water says whether water still reaches the soil. When it is none with a phrase, say that no water has reached the soil since then, and point to the irrigation where the pattern does: whether water reaches this plant for one node, the line from its start to the last plant for a cluster, the irrigation schedule and the water supply for the whole farm.
When soil_water is arriving, say that the soil still gets water. For one node or a cluster, suggest checking the plants for heat damage, pests or root problems. For the whole farm, the heat is the cause, so suggest longer or more frequent irrigation.
For equipment faults, fault says what the data shows. For missing data, say that the sensors have sent no data and that the plants they cover are not monitored. For implausible values, say that the sensor gives values that look wrong. For camera view changed, say that the camera no longer sees the plant’s leaves.
For faults, point to where to look: the node’s power and connection for one node, the power supply its nodes share for a cluster, the gateway and its power supply for the whole farm.
For severe items, say that the action is for today.
Be plain, friendly and direct. No greeting, no sign-off, no explanation of the monitoring.
Keep the whole message under 600 characters.

title: Teacher prompt
text:
Writing messages
teach sends the prompt and one record to the teacher through fastllm, which also reaches other providers and llama.cpp’s OpenAI-compatible server, so the baseline and fine-tuned models can go through the same client later. Each call gets a fresh chat, so records never see each other. A temperature of 0.3 keeps the messages consistent and still varies their wording. Haiku is the teacher, as the scope’s Choice of teacher section explains, and model selects another one.
teach returns the message with its provenance, as the Choice of teacher section requires: the model, the temperature, the prompt version and the date. The prompt version is a short hash of the system prompt, so messages written with different prompts are never compared by mistake.

title: Coffee water stress
text: In the field, the triage comes from code in the domain project: feature engineering and an ML model flag the nodes to watch or fix for one farm and one day. The SLM turns that triage into a WhatsApp message for the farmer, as the scope describes. This module generates synthetic triage records, so that we can build and evaluate the message side before the real triage exists. It generates them in code, without a language model, so every record is valid and a seed reproduces it.

title: Coffee water stress
text:
Dimensions
The task has three dimensions with three levels each. A tuple sets the main item of a record: the kind of problem, its spatial pattern and its severity. For both, the record holds at least one item of each kind.


Exported source

Farm layout
A farm is a list of groups of nodes, each group sharing an irrigation line. The names follow one of three schemes, drawn at random: greenhouse benches (small farms, 4 to 16 nodes), blocks with drip lines, or numbered plots (12 to 80 nodes). Location names are what the farmer reads, so they never contain node IDs.

title: Coffee water stress
text:
Causes and onset
Each item reports what the data shows about its cause, never a part that no sensor watches. For water stress, soil_water says whether water still reaches the soil: arriving, or none with the time since the soil last got water, which is never later than the start of the stress. Water that stops arriving is the commoner case, about 70% of items. For equipment faults, fault says what the data shows. Moderate and severe faults are always missing data, by the scope’s definition of fault severity. An early fault on a single node can also be implausible values from one sensor, or a camera whose view has changed; on several nodes at once, an early fault is missing data, since one shared cause is far likelier than many sensors failing in the same way.


Exported source

Severity also sets how long ago the problem started. ONSET gives the range of days for each kind and severity. For faults it follows the scope’s definition: no readings for 1 to 3 days is moderate, and more than 3 days is severe.
The record gives the start as a phrase that the message can use as it is, so that neither the teacher nor the SLM has to work out weekdays from dates: since today, since yesterday, since a weekday within the past week, or for a week or more.

text:
Items
One item is one problem at one location. A one node item names a node, a cluster item names a group, and a widespread item covers the whole farm with more than 70% of its nodes flagged. used holds the locations already taken in the record, so that two items never point at the same group.
Messages give no counts, so a cluster or widespread item carries an amount word for the share of its group’s nodes that are flagged: all, almost all (80% or more), most (more than half) or some (half or fewer). The triage computes it, so that neither the teacher nor the SLM does arithmetic:

title: Coffee water stress
text:
Triage records
triage is the generator for sample. It builds the main item from the tuple, then adds random variation: the farm and its layout, a day in the Brazilian dry season (May to September), and up to two extra items. Extra items are never more severe than the main one, and are single nodes or clusters. Together, the single nodes and clusters of one kind stay below the widespread threshold: on a small farm, two clusters that flag almost every node would really be one widespread problem, such as a gateway fault. For both, the first extra item is of the other kind. Items are sorted most severe first, so that the message can keep their order. A node that sends no readings cannot be flagged for water stress, so when a both tuple is widespread and moderate or severe, its widespread item is the water stress and the fault is the extra item. The record holds no weather: in the field, weather is an input to the ML model, and its effect shows in severity and in soil_water.

A test set
The test set has 10 records per tuple, 270 in total:

test_eq(set(Counter(tuple(r['tuple'].values()) for r in recs).values()), {10})

Every record keeps the rules above. The main item matches its tuple, no item is more severe than the tuple, items are sorted most severe first, every location appears once, both records hold both kinds, no water stress item sits beside a widespread fault that loses data, and the single nodes and clusters of one kind never add up to a widespread item. Each item carries the cause fields of its kind, and nothing else about its cause:

    test_eq((main['pattern'], main['severity']), (t['pattern'], t['severity']))
    assert all(sev(it['severity']) <= sev(t['severity']) for it in items(r))
    test_eq(len({it['location'] for it in items(r)}), len(items(r)))
    if t['problem'] == 'both': test_eq({it['problem'] for it in items(r)}, set(KINDS))
    ps = {(it['problem'], it['pattern'], it['severity'] != 'early') for it in items(r)}
    if ('equipment fault', 'widespread', True) in ps: assert all(p != 'water stress' for p, *_ in ps)
    assert all(_flagged(items(r), k) < _wide(r['input']['nodes']) for k in KINDS)
    test_eq([sev(it['severity']) for it in items(r)], sorted((sev(it['severity']) for it in items(r)), reverse=True))
    for it in items(r):

        if 'nodes_flagged' in it: test_eq(it.get('amount'), amount(it['nodes_flagged'], it['nodes_in_group']))
